Afazuddin Mollah &others ----- Appellants
Vs.

full_judgment:
3. The opposite parties i.e. the present appellants, filed written objection before the Administrator of Waqfs contending, inter alia, that they purchased the lands from the sons and heirs of the alleged Waqif Aynuddin Munshi through a number of registered sale-deeds in between 1951-1952 for valuable consideration without notice and since then they have been possessing the disputed lands i.e. for more than 33 years on mutation of their names on payment of rents thereof and as the property in question was not at all Waqf-property and the same was recorded as secular property. It was alleged in the written objection that the property not being the Waqf property, the application under section 64(1) of the Waqfs ordinance was not maintainable. It was further alleged that the opposite parties were not at all aware of any Waqf of this property until the receipt of notice of the show cause in respect of the application under section 64(1) of the Waqfs ordinance from the office of the Administrator of Waqfs and on query they found that the Waqf-deed was executed by the father of their vendors of the disputed property on 16.7.1948 and registered on 17.7.1948 by fraudulent means. It was further alleged that the said Aynuddin Munshi was about 95 years of age and he was seriously ailing and in such situation he was taken to the house of his son-in-law, one Ishaque Ali, and therefrom in collusion with one Syeduddin he was taken to the Registration office and the alleged deed of Waqf was created and subsequently registered on the following day without the intention and free will of the said Aynuddin Munshi who was not even within his full sense because of his old age and illness at the relevant time. Thereafter when the said Aynuddin Munshi came to his proper senses and realised that a fraudulent waqf-deed was created in his name, he executed and registered a deed of cancellation of the said Waqf on 20.9.48, though written wrongly in the impugned judgment as 17.7.1948 of the said Waqf deed. It was further alleged that in fact, the said Aynuddin Munshi executed a deed of gift in respect of the said properties in favour of his 2 sons and the said deed of gift was, of course, registered on 15.2.49 who thereafter transferred these lands in favour of the opposite parties, the present appellants by a number of registered sale deeds in between 1951-1952 and since then these appellants have been possessing the same after completion of mutation in their names and on payment of rents thereof and further during SA and RS operations their names have been recorded in the recent khatians and the nature of the lands has been shown as secular property. The present appellants as opposite parties in that proceeding filed the relevant deeds of purchase, mutation Khatians, rent receipts, etc. The learned Administrator of Waqfs after hearing both the sides found that the said Waqf Estate was enrolled as Waqf-ul-Awlad on 2.7.49 on the petition submitted by Md. Ishaque Munshi, the son-in-law of the alleged Waqif but after enrolment no one approached the Administrator of Waqfs for appointment as a subsequent Mutwalli till 8.2.83 and further there was no record upto 7.2.83 of the management of the said Waqf Estate. He therefore observed that after enrolment of the Waqf Estate, it was not acted upon. He also found that the Waqf-deed was cancelled by a registered deed on 17.7.48 by the Waqif and since then the father of the petitioner Mobarak Ali Munshi, the alleged Mutwalli and others, the present appellants i.e. opposite parties, are in actual possession of the property for the last 33 years on payment of rents. It has been argued on behalf of the opposite party-appellants that the theory that' once a Waqf is always a Waqf was not justified in this case and further the alleged Waqif Aynuddin Munshi gifted away the said property by a registered deed which was executed on 15.7.1948 before the creation of the alleged Waqf and no step was taken by the petitioner Mutwalli or any earlier Mutwalli for cancellation of the said deed of gift. 

 14. The learned Advocate for the appellants further argued that the learned District Judge also committed error of law in coming to a finding that the Waqf was acted upon only in view of the fact that it was enrolled at the instance of one Ishaque Ali, son-in-law of the Waqif and that after the creation of the Waqf, the Waqif divested himself of the lands in question absolutely for ever and he had no right of revocation or cancellation of the Waqf. The learned Advocate further submits that mere enrolment of the waqf could not be a conclusive proof of the fact that the waqf was valid and it was acted upon. He further submits that the theory that 'once a waqf is always a waqf is not also applicable in all cases and, as such, a waqf unless is found to be valid and lawful one, it cannot claim immunity from challenge. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate has relied on a decision in the case of Syed Masud Ali and others Vs. Md. Asmatullah and others reported in 31 DLR (AD) 249. However, I feel that to establish valid waqf, the intention of the waqif to make such Waqf must be fully established. It is contended on behalf of the appellants that the learned District Judge failed to notice the averments of the wakif as made in the deed of cancellation, of course those averments require to be proved by evidence of witness or witnesses. Even if a valid Waqf once made cannot be revoked or cancelled, yet the deed of cancellation of the Waqf in question filed in this case by the appellants may be taken into consideration along with other evidence, if any, in order to see whether the wakif in fact had the real intention to make the said waqf. It is further contended by the learned Advocate for the appellants that the appellants acquired the property in question through valid purchase by registered deeds from the heirs of the said Waqif Aynuddin Munshi and there was mutation of the Joma in the Khatian thereafter and the land in question was recorded in the names of the appellants in the SA and the RS Khatians as secular properties and they have been possessing the same for more than 33 years, but the learned District Judge did not consider this aspect of the matter and the documents filed by the appellants in connection therewith. It is further contended that even if there was a valid Waqf, yet it was not acted upon as has been found by the Administrator of Waqfs and that the character of the land as waqf property was also lost by adverse possession of the opposite parties-appellants. Hence it is submitted that the property having lost its Waqf character, no application under section 64(1) of the Waqfs ordinance for eviction of the opposite parties could lie at all. Besides, the learned District Judge before passing an order of eviction, must come to a finding that the occupants, here the opposite parties, are trespassers or strangers in the disputed land. There is no doubt that in the case of an application under the provisions of section 64(1) of the Waqfs ordinance, the determination of the Waqf character of the land is very much material before passing any order of eviction or rejection and for this there is provision under section 50 of the Waqfs ordinance to determine the character of the property in dispute. Section 50 runs thus: 

 "The petitioner is possessing the lands by virtue of a deed of purchase dated 9.1.71 and that the RS Khatian and SA Khatians and subsequent record of right stand in his name and or in the name of his predecessor. Therefore it is difficult to hold that the petitioner was a trespasser in the land in question. But the Mutwalli claims the property in question to be the property of Waqf Estate. The Administrator of Waqfs is authorised to determine the nature and character of Waqf property under section 50 of the Waqfs ordinance 1962. Before exercising the powers under section 64(1) of the said ordinance, the Administrator should have taken resort to the provision of section 50 of the ordinance in cases where complicated questions relating to title or possession are involved. The Administrator of Waqfs having powers to determine the question as to nature of the Waqf property to the exclusion of the jurisdiction of Civil Court such power should not have been 'exercised casually without taking greater care and caution."
